h: Stem, stern and a starring role in Outlander
p: The ship nickname isn't just about the outline. The towers have even picked up ship-style names: the north tower, poking out into the water, is known as the stem tower, the south tower is the stern, and the central tower sits in the middle like a main mast. Walk from one end to the other and you're effectively walking the deck.

Outlander fans will know it straight away as Fort William, the grim garrison where the villainous Black Jack Randall holds sway. Film buffs might also recognise it from Franco Zeffirelli's 1990 version of Hamlet starring Mel Gibson. Standing in the courtyard, you can see why location scouts love it.

Later in its life, from the 1870s, Blackness became an army ammunition depot, which is when the pier jutting out into the Forth was added. That use carried on into the early twentieth century, so the castle's story runs from medieval power games right up to the age of modern warfare.
An hour or so is enough for most visitors, maybe a bit more if you're taking photos or letting the kids explore every nook.

The John Muir Way runs along this stretch of the Forth, so you can walk west towards Bo'ness, home of the Bo'ness and Kinneil Railway, a heritage steam line that's great for families. Head east instead and Hopetoun House, one of Scotland's grandest stately homes, is just along the shore. A bit further on, South Queensferry is the place to see all three Forth bridges side by side, a cracking finale to the day.
